newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Euro MP says Romania's Iliescu rigging election.
newsitem.headline: Euro MP says Romania's Iliescu rigging election.

text.p: Romania's presidential and general election campaign turned increasingly nasty on Wednesday with a senior Dutch member of the European parliament accusing President Ion Iliescu of trying to rig the outcome.

Iliescu's party denied the charge and said it amounted to blatant interference in the November 3 poll. The president, who has run Romania since the 1989 overthrow of communism, heads a field of 16 candidates in opinion polls.
Wim van Velzen, Dutch president of the European Union of Christian Democrats, denounced Iliescu's conduct in the campaign after a visit this week to the Balkan country.
He said basic democracy was at issue seven years after the execution of Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
"This is not a serious way for a European country to behave -- the manipulations of President Iliescu are quite brazen," van Velzen said in a statement from Brussels.
"The elections are a month away. There is still time to ensure at least some semblance of a real election."
Contacted later by telephone, van Velzen said Iliescu had failed in six years of office to achieve his aim of creating conditions for Romania's integration into Western institutions.
"I am not engaged in a personal fight with Mr Iliescu," he said. "My only concern is that democracy and prosperity should develop in Romania and things are not going well."
Iliescu portrays himself as a guarantor of stability in the campaign, the third presidential race in six years.

The only two rivals given any chance of unseating him say Iliescu and his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) embody Romania's unhappy past, while sharing his view that Romania must pursue market reforms and move towards eventual membership of NATO and the European Union.
Surveys give Iliescu 34 percent support in the first round, well short of the 50 precent needed to win without a run-off.
Behind him are Emil Constantinescu, head of the Democratic Convention grouping 15 parties and Petre Roman, a Social Democrat who was Romania's first post-communist prime minister.
The polls also say the PDSR could well lose its place as parliament's largest party.
A PDSR statement denounced comments made by van Velzen even before he had left the country, saying they "defied the norms of good manners, politics and his own country".

"The PDSR protests against the arrogant way in which a European organisation is openly interfering in our election campaign," the party said. "There is a worrying phenomenon here -- that of seeking legitimacy through foreign support."
Iliescu's rivals accuse the PDSR of staging a fake opinion poll with loaded questions to win over wavering voters. The PDSR denies the poll was biased.
Human rights groups have accused authorities of harrassing journalists who helped expose it by forcing their way into a building where the telephone poll was being conducted.
The opposition also denounces an Iliescu campaign video which accusing Constantinescu of seeking to restore the monarchy -- by superimposing his portrait on that of exiled King Michael.
Politicians of all persuasions said rules allowing voters to cast ballots by producing either identity papers or voters' cards were certain to cause mass fraud and multiple voting.
Parliament rushed through legislation this week requiring returning officers to stamp each voter's identity card.
